description: Believing `where` returns an Array of records immediately, rather than a lazy ActiveRecord::Relation that only queries the database when enumerated, counted, or inspected.
Believing `find`, `find_by`, and `where(...).first` behave identically — not realising `find` raises RecordNotFound on a missing id while `find_by` returns nil.
Believing `save` and `update` raise an exception when validations fail, instead of returning false; only the bang versions (`save!`, `update!`) raise.
Believing `record.errors` is populated without running validations — not realising `valid?` (or a save attempt) must run first to refresh the errors object.
Believing `update_attribute` runs validations like `update` does, when it skips validations (though it does run callbacks and touches updated_at).
Believing `update_column`/`update_columns` run validations and callbacks and bump updated_at, when they write straight to the database, skipping all of them.
Believing `validates_uniqueness_of` guarantees uniqueness, when it is a read-then-write check subject to races and requires a database unique index for real safety.
Believing `validates :x, presence: true` only rejects nil, when it rejects any blank value including empty strings, whitespace, and empty arrays — and that `false` passes presence.
Believing request params arrive as integers, booleans, or dates; in fact query and form params are strings (or hashes/arrays of strings) until explicitly cast.
Believing `permit` validates or sanitises values, when it only whitelists which keys may be mass-assigned; it performs no type checking or escaping.
Confusing `params.require(:user)` with `params.permit(:user)` — thinking `require` whitelists attributes or that `permit` raises when a key is missing.
Believing `redirect_to` or `render` immediately returns from the controller action, when execution continues and a second render/redirect raises DoubleRenderError.
Believing `render :edit` changes the browser URL like a redirect, when it only renders a template in the current request without a new HTTP round trip.
Believing `includes` and `joins` are interchangeable — not realising `joins` builds an INNER JOIN for filtering while `includes` preloads associations to avoid N+1.
Believing that looping over records and calling an association inside the loop issues one query, rather than one query per record (the N+1 problem).
Believing `count`, `size`, and `length` on a relation or association are identical, ignoring that `count` always queries, `length` loads all records, and `size` depends on load state.
Believing `pluck` returns model objects like `select` does, when it returns raw column values as an array and bypasses model instantiation and methods.
Believing `default_scope` only affects explicit queries, when it also leaks into associations, `new` defaults, and `unscoped` workarounds, making it hard to opt out of.
Believing a scope body may be a plain expression, when a non-lambda body (e.g. `where('created_at > ?', Time.now)`) is evaluated once at class load and freezes the value.
Believing the foreign key lives on the `has_many` side — not realising the table declaring `belongs_to` is the one that holds the `*_id` column.
Believing `belongs_to` is optional by default; in modern Rails it adds a presence validation unless `optional: true` is given.
Believing associated records are deleted automatically when a parent is destroyed, when nothing happens without `dependent: :destroy`/`:delete_all` or a database-level cascade.
Believing `delete`/`delete_all` run destroy callbacks and `dependent` options like `destroy`/`destroy_all`, when they issue raw DELETE statements and skip model logic.
Believing `has_many :through` works without the intermediate association or model, or confusing it with `has_and_belongs_to_many`, which has no join model at all.
Believing `Model.new` or building through an association writes to the database, when only `create`/`save` persist and `new` leaves the record unpersisted.
Believing `parent.children.build` saves at once, or that `parent.children.create` on an unsaved parent persists — ignoring how autosave defers child writes.
Believing `after_save`/`after_create` run outside the transaction so external jobs and emails see committed data; that requires `after_commit`.
Believing returning `false` from a before_* callback cancels the operation, when modern Rails requires `throw :abort` to halt the callback chain.
Believing a transaction rolls back when a block returns false or a save fails, when rollback requires a raised exception (or `raise ActiveRecord::Rollback`).
Believing editing an already-run migration changes the schema on the next `db:migrate`, when Rails tracks applied versions and skips them; a new migration or rollback is needed.
Believing models read columns from migration files, when the authoritative source is the database (and `schema.rb`), so a forgotten `db:migrate` leaves methods missing.
Believing each database column needs an `attr_accessor` or explicit attribute declaration, when ActiveRecord defines accessors from the table schema automatically.
Misreading `resources :posts`: believing it creates no show/edit routes, or that route order is irrelevant, when the first matching route wins and member/collection blocks matter.
Believing `post_path` and `post_url` are interchangeable, or that a named helper works without the matching route — ignoring that `_url` includes the host and is needed in emails.
Believing controller instance variables or memoised class-level state persist across requests, when each request gets a fresh controller instance and class state is shared unsafely.
Believing local variables from a controller action or from one partial are visible in views and other partials, when only instance variables and explicit `locals:` are passed.
Believing `html_safe` sanitises user input, when it merely marks a string as trusted and disables escaping, opening an XSS hole; `sanitize` is the sanitiser.
Believing CSRF tokens are unnecessary for JavaScript or API-style requests from the app's own pages, so disabling `protect_from_forgery` is a harmless fix for 422 errors.
Believing behaviour seen in development carries over to production, ignoring differences in eager loading, class reloading, caching, asset compilation, and error reporting.
Believing `Time.now`/`Date.today` respect the application time zone, when zone-aware code needs `Time.current`/`Time.zone.now`/`Date.current`.
